Backend & Database Supabase vs Firebase Source review recorded 2026-11-14 · 5 min read

Supabase vs Firebase

Realtime fan-out is metered on both platforms. The hypothetical 4.32 billion monthly deliveries imply $1,296 in Firestore Standard read charges or $10,787.50 in Supabase Realtime message overage, before other costs. The old flat-$25 comparison was wrong; neither estimate proves the workload fits.

Verdict

The flat-$25 realtime comparison is withdrawn. For the stated hypothetical fan-out, Supabase message overage alone is $10,787.50 versus $1,296 in Firestore Standard read charges; both exclude other costs. Choose using complete regional bills, feature requirements and measured capacity, not the presence or absence of a database per-read fee.

1. Two billing models, both with usage meters

Correction, November 14, 2026: this article previously treated Supabase Postgres Changes as unmetered and compared a high-fan-out workload with a flat $25 project. Supabase bills Realtime Messages separately from database compute, so that conclusion is withdrawn.

A database query and delivery of a Realtime change are different billing events. Supabase combines plan, compute and usage charges; Firestore Standard meters document operations, among other items.

MeterPublished unitScope
Firestore Standard reads$0.03/100,000us-central1, not every edition or region
Firestore Standard writes$0.09/100,000Same regional model
Supabase Realtime5M messages included on Pro, then $2.50/MOrganization allowance; excess rounded up in 1M packages
Supabase Pro Micro base$25 + $10 − $10 creditOne project, excludes usage overage

2. Model deliveries before comparing prices

Assume 50 clients continuously watch the same 100 documents; every document changes 20 times/minute for 30 days. Each change reaches all 50 clients, with no coalescing, filtering or missed deliveries.

50 × 100 × 20 × 60 × 24 × 30 = 4.32 billion deliveries. Firestore Standard read-only gross cost at the stated rate is $1,296. This is arithmetic, not a load-test result.

Firestore bills listener additions and updates, plus removals caused by document changes; deleting a document does not itself add a listener read. Reconnects can reissue billed queries: always with offline persistence disabled, or after more than 30 minutes disconnected with it enabled.

Initial reads, reconnects, security-rule and index reads, storage, transfer and taxes are omitted. The underlying 86.4M updates would also incur writes: $77.76 gross at $0.09/100,000. Daily free quotas must be applied by day; unused quota is not a monthly pool.

3. Supabase messages, spend caps and throughput are separate

Postgres Changes counts one message per receiving client: one change delivered to 50 clients means 50 messages. Broadcast also counts the send plus each receiving client; Presence has its own traffic, so do not substitute one meter for another.

At 4.32B delivered messages, ceil((4.32B − 5M)/1M) × $2.50 = $10,787.50 overage. Adding the illustrative $25 Pro Micro base gives $10,812.50, before extra compute, egress, connections or other usage.

The model averages 1,666.7 deliveries/s. Published Pro limits are 500 messages/s, or 2,500/s for Pro without a spend cap; peak connections are 500 or 10,000 respectively. These are Realtime limits, not database pooler connections.

A spend cap covers Realtime quota overage: leaving it on can restrict service, not grant unlimited free delivery. Turning it off permits charges but does not remove throughput limits or prove capacity; validate burst load, payloads, RLS work and actual project settings.

4. Index entry reads are the Firestore line item nobody quotes

  • One read per batch of up to 1,000 index entries a query reads.
  • A query with one range field pays nothing for index entries. Zero range fields are also exempt. Add a second range field and billing starts.
  • count(), sum() and avg() bill index reads, with a 1-document-read minimum even at zero entries.

Firestore's own docs give the example: count() over 1,500 index entries bills 2 document reads.

Ten million plain reads cost $3.00 at the listed rate. The count() in your page header is a different bill.

Audit any query that combines two range fields before it ships.

5. Migration is a schema project with a script attached

supabase-community/firebase-to-supabase on GitHub is community tooling, not an official CLI. It exports collections and loads tables; splitting nested JSON into related tables needs custom hooks.

Auth is the sharper edge. firestoreusers2json and import_users move users, importing hashes with Firestore's SCRYPT parameters (base64_signer_key, base64_salt_separator, rounds, mem_cost).

Verifying an existing Firebase password on first login needs a middleware the repo itself marks work in progress. The AWS Lambda variant is listed as TBD.

Until that middleware exists, plan for blocked logins at cutover and decide in advance whether you force a password reset.

6. Compare complete bills and prove capacity

Do not choose either platform from the old $1,296-versus-$25 headline. The corrected model makes Supabase message overage much larger than the Firestore read line, but neither is a full bill or performance guarantee.

  1. Measure changes, actual recipients, payload sizes, active hours and reconnects.
  2. Include Supabase Realtime packages and other usage, not only Postgres compute.
  3. Include Firestore writes, query/security-rule reads, storage and network costs for the selected region and edition.
  4. Load-test throughput, burst behavior and authorization overhead before sizing a project.
  5. Consider batching, narrower subscriptions or lower update frequency when product requirements allow.

Firestore free allowances include 50,000 reads, 20,000 writes and 20,000 deletes daily, plus storage/network quotas. Supabase’s included Realtime quota is also finite; check consumption across the organization.

Code and configuration

Supabase 
// Relational read in one round trip. Free-tier note:
// the nested select is a JOIN, so 50 comments cost 0 extra reads.
const { data, error } = await supabase
  .from('posts')
  .select('id, title, comments(id, body, user_id)')
  .eq('published', true)
  .order('created_at', { ascending: false })
  .limit(20);
// Here it breaks: anon key + missing RLS policy = empty array, not an error.
if (error) throw error;
Firebase 
// N+1 by design: comments are a second query per post.
const q = query(collection(db, 'posts'), where('published', '==', true));
const snap = await getDocs(q);           // 20 reads
for (const doc of snap.docs) {
  // Denormalise, or pay: 20 more queries = 20 more billed reads
  const comments = await getDocs(collection(doc.ref, 'comments'));
}
// Here it breaks: a live listener on this collection bills a read on
// every document update, for every listener, for as long as the tab is open.

What you gain, what you give up

Supabase

You gain
  • SQL queries do not have a per-read charge; Realtime delivery and other usage are separately metered
  • pgvector lives in the same Postgres as your rows, so RAG needs no second system
  • Standard Postgres: SQL, JOINs, transactions, triggers, and pg_dump as an exit door
  • The connection ceiling is purchasable: 200 pooled connections on $10 Micro up to 12,000 on $3,730
You give up
  • Compute capacity and metered usage both matter; Realtime quotas and throughput limits are separate
  • Every extra project adds its own compute line ($10 for a Micro) even on one Pro plan
  • Free projects are paused after a week of inactivity, which kills demo and staging projects
  • Realtime has published message-rate and connection limits; database pooler capacity is separate

Firebase

You gain
  • Offline persistence and multi-platform SDKs that work when the network does not
  • No connection pool to size: events are metered, not sockets
  • A daily free quota of 50,000 reads and 20,000 writes per project
  • Listeners meter additions, updates and change-driven removals; initial queries and reconnects can add reads
You give up
  • A dashboard left open all day is a recurring read charge: 50 users can pass $1,296/month
  • Reconnects are billed like brand-new queries — with persistence off, every one of them
  • Index entry reads are a second meter: a second range field starts billing
  • No JOIN, and the export tool flattens one collection to one table, so schema design lands on you

Migration path

What switching actually takes

supabase-community/firebase-to-supabase is community tooling, not an official CLI. firestore2json.js exports one collection, json2supabase.js loads it into one table, and fields are flattened to text, numeric, boolean or jsonb — splitting nested JSON into related tables is a hook you write. Auth is the harder half: firestoreusers2json and import_users carry passwords over as SCRYPT hash parameters, and verifying a user's existing Firebase password on first login needs middleware the repo still marks work in progress. Budget the schema work, not the script.

Common questions

Is Supabase Postgres Changes free once I pay $25?
No. Pro includes 5 million Realtime Messages; database changes count once per receiving client. Excess is $2.50 per million-message package, rounded up. Compute, network and other usage can add charges.
Does offset pagination save reads on Firestore?
No. Firestore bills a read for every skipped document, so offset 10 returning 1 document costs 11 reads.
Does disabling the Supabase spend cap guarantee this load works?
No. It permits billable overage for covered usage, while throughput limits remain. Published Pro limits are 500 messages/s with the cap and 2,500/s without it. The example averages 1,666.7 deliveries/s, but peak traffic, payloads, RLS checks and compute capacity still require testing.
How is Firestore vector search billed?
kNN vector search bills one read per batch of up to 100 vector index entries. That is a tenth of the 1,000-entry batch size used for regular index entry reads.
